newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kinshasa braces for anti-Mobutu protest shutdown.
newsitem.headline: Kinshasa braces for anti-Mobutu protest shutdown.

text.p: Zaire's militant opposition headed for a possible confrontation with troops in Kinshasa on Monday by organising a stay-at-home protest to try to force President Mobutu Sese Seko from office.
Mobutu's 32-year rule faced a twin threat from rebels closing in from the east and south and from a Kinshasa-based opposition emboldened by the guerrilla advances.

Laurent Kabila's rebels said at their headquarters in the eastern city of Goma that they were resuming their offensive after a three-day pause to allow Mombutu to step down honourably. Mobutu ignored their Sunday deadline.
Authorities in Kinshasa declared that Monday's dead-city action by the opposition was an infringement of emergency rule clamped on the vast Central African country by Mobutu last week.
The general appointed prime minister by Mobutu to enforce emergency rule vowed that troops would deal with militants stopping people from going to work, but the opposition played down the threat.
"Tomorrow is a dead city. Nobody will be on the streets, so if the army wants to intervene they will have to go find people in their homes," opposition spokesman Laurent Mbayo said on Sunday.
Supporters of radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi, angered by his sacking last week only after a few days in office as prime minister, were preparing for the worst.
Taxi drivers said they saw youths gathering piles of tyres to be used as flaming barricades. "We don't know what will happen tomorrow," one driver said.
Residents of the city of over five million people scrambled to stock up with supplies, sending prices soaring in markets and the handful of shops that opened on Sunday.
"People have been stocking up since yesterday," said Mauritanian storeowner Sidi Mohamed.

His compatriot Mohamed Umar next door said shops were running out of imports. "Suppliers are not bringing in goods. We too are not buying because you don't know if your shop will be looted the next day," he said.
He said prices of imported food had shot up in the few days since Kabila's forces seized Zaire's copper capital of Lubumbashi and set their sights on Kinshasa.
Kinshasa's military governor intervened on the lunchtime national television news on Sunday to urge people to remain calm.
"An atmosphere of panic, due essentially to the situation in the east of our country, reigns among Kinshasa's men and women," General Amela Lokima said.
"The most fantastic rumours according to which the city of Kinshasa would soon fall to the armed rebellion are gaining ground."
Lokima said the army was ready to defend Kinshasa, adding, "The security of our capital is our fundamental duty."

Mobutu's collapsing army has been unable to check the rebel offensive that began near Zaire's eastern border last October. Kabila's forces now hold more than half the country including most major centres outside Kinshasa.
